    Dr. Ali Shtarbanov’s Vision for Maximizing SNU Robotics’ Global Impact

    ← 소식 전체 보기

    What SNU Robotics Institute can Learn from the MIT Media Lab.

    Dr. Ali Shtarbanov received his PhD from the MIT Media Lab and joined the SNU Robotics Institute in September as its first postdoctoral fellow. His doctoral research in Human-Computer Interaction focused on designing hardware development platforms and deploying technological ecosystems that foster creativity, innovation, and interdisciplinary collaboration. He has also worked at Meta Reality Labs and IBM Research. During his PhD, he developed a framework for creating highly impactful, general-purpose platform technologies and maximizing their impact by building ecosystems around them. He developed multiple hardware and software platforms, including FlowIO, SoftRobotics.IO, SleeveIO, and ModiStrap, along with dozens of application-oriented projects enabled by them. Among these, FlowIO, together with the SoftRobotics.IO ecosystem built around it, has grown into a widely recognized platform that has been used by researchers, designers, and engineers at more than 100 universities and institutions around the world, including Stanford, Harvard, Cornell, ETH Zurich, Imperial College London, NUS, NTU, and Tsinghua University, as well as at companies such as Meta Reality Labs, Toyota Research Institute, and several startups. The projects enabled by his work have spanned numerous fields and domains, including soft robotics, haptics, interactive interfaces, assistive technology, human-robot interaction, automotive applications, as well as education, art, and design. His work has enabled multiple master's theses, art exhibitions, and dozens of published research projects across these domains, while giving Dr. Shtarbanov the opportunity to collaborate with more than 150 people from diverse backgrounds and institutions. Among the recognition he has received for his work are the Hackaday Grand Prize, the world’s largest open-source engineering competition; the Grand Prize at the Create the Future Design Contest, organized by NASA’s Tech Briefs magazine; the top prize at the ACM CHI Student Research Competition; and multiple design awards, including an iF Design Award. Most recently, he received the Brain Pool Fellowship, Korea’s premier fellowship for outstanding overseas scientists, through a competitive research proposal process administered by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Research Foundation of Korea.

    Dr. Shtarbanov brings a unique perspective to the SNU Robotics Institute, combining the highly impactful, interdisciplinary research culture of the MIT Media Lab with his own experience developing platforms and ecosystems that have enabled technologies to spread across fields, institutions, and applications. He has a concrete vision for applying this combined approach to help shape the SNU Robotics Institute into a globally impactful, interdisciplinary institution that goes beyond developing great robotic technologies and publishing in top journals to developing and deploying entire ecosystems that enable these technologies to reach and be extended by thousands of people across diverse fields, while fostering highly interdisciplinary international collaborations.

    Dr. Shtarbanov first learned about SNU when he met Professor Kyujin Cho at an IROS soft robotics workshop in 2023, where they were both giving invited talks. He was deeply inspired by the diversity of robotics projects Professor Cho presented and immediately began imagining numerous new applications for the technologies.

    “I remember thinking about all the new applications those technologies could be used for, especially if they were extended into platforms and made more widely accessible for people to obtain, replicate, or extend. I saw an entire space of possibilities for how those robotics projects could be used in other domains, such as HCI, interactive interfaces, and art."

    “Many of my colleagues from other fields would absolutely love to know about these projects and use them in their own creative work. Why are they not more widely known outside of the domain of robotics? We could do so much with them and extend them in so many different directions.”

    After the workshop, Professor Cho invited him to visit his lab at SNU and see the projects in person. Two years later, in December 2025, Dr. Shtarbanov finally had the opportunity to visit Korea and SNU while doing an international speaking tour. He was so delighted by the experience that he extended his stay in Korea to a full month.

    “The research was incredibly inspiring, the people were brilliant, and I received a very warm welcome from everyone I met at SNU. I was also incredibly impressed by the facilities and equipment available, which matched or even exceeded those I had access to at MIT.”

    He also enjoyed SNU’s scenic campus and many aspects of living in Korea. More importantly, he envisioned numerous ways to collaborate with SNU researchers: deploying existing projects, extending them into platforms, and building entire ecosystems around them.

    “I see enormous potential in the technologies developed at SNU to reach a far wider and broader impact beyond publications, outside the domain of robotics, and across fields—and I want to work with people at SNU to unlock that impact potential.”

    “Impact”—a word that initially puzzled people at SNU

    Dr. Shtarbanov used the word “impact” far more often than “research.” Impact is hardly an unfamiliar term to researchers at SNU. If anything, it is a word they are required to include in almost every research proposal. Researchers often struggle to imagine and describe “impact” before their work has even begun, as though the research were about to lead immediately to commercialization or a startup.

    For people accustomed to writing those ambitious projections, his insistence that researchers should think more deeply about impact was, frankly, somewhat puzzling.

    But the impact he describes is not a grand promise written in advance of the research. Nor is he saying that every paper must immediately lead to technology transfer or a startup. Those outcomes, he explains, happen in stages. To him, impact is closer to the work that begins after the paper is published.

    So what does he mean by impact, particularly in the context of a technological project?

    Broadly speaking, he says there are at least three factors by which he defines the true impact a technology project. The first is the number of users or beneficiaries served by the project. The second is the number of use cases or utilities the project offers. A technology that serves five different needs, for example, has greater impact potential than a technology that serves only one, all else being equal.

    The third factor is the number of progenies it enables. If a project engenders new discoveries and new projects, it creates what he calls a “posterity impact.” Its impact includes not only those immediate progenies, but also the future generations of work that they enable.

    According to his philosophy of impact, the most impactful projects are therefore those that maximize all three components: beneficiaries, utilities, and progenies. The examples he gives include building blocks like the transistors, or tools and platforms like Raspberry PI, Arduino, and Scratch.

    Research that Creates Ecosystems not just Publications

    At first, it is easy to interpret his argument as a call to communicate good research more actively. Indeed, at the MIT Media Lab, researchers often build entire websites around many projects and give talks across many different venues, both academic and non-acadmic ones.

    This is not about publicity, showing off, or building an individual researcher’s reputation among the general public. If a new piece of knowledge has been recognized through publication, researchers who do not read that particular journal may still need to know about it.

    If the project is a robot, a materials scientist might see it and try a new material. A designer might create a different form. An artist or educator might discover an application that the original researcher had never considered. Research has to reach people outside the journal’s immediate readership before connections across entirely different fields can begin.

    But the impact Dr. Shtarbanov describes goes beyond communication. Publishing a project website and giving talks are not enough. For research to be used and extended by others, communities, deployment models, infrastructure, and supporting technologies must also be developed around it. This is what he calls an “ecosystem.”

    “To maximize the impact potential of one’s work, it is important to look beyond publications. Instead of taking a publication-centric approach, one should take an ecosystem-centric approach. The new technology that is developed is only one component of an ecosystem.”

    Why did Scratch and LEGO Mindstorms become better known than their papers?

    Dr. Shtarbanov points to Scratch and LEGO Mindstorms as two widely-known projects associated with the MIT Media Lab. Scratch, a programming environment designed for children, is now widely used to introduce coding to elementary school students, including in Korea. Almost everyone interested in technology knows Scratch, yet relatively few people have read the academic publications behind it. The same applies to LEGO Mindstorms.

    “If we consider some of the most well-known Media Lab projects, such as Scratch or LEGO Mindstorms, they did not become impactful because they were published in a top journal. You have probably never even heard of any of the publications about those projects. And it was not just because of publicity either. Rather, it was because entire ecosystems were built, developed, and deployed around those works.”

    FlowIO was also designed not merely as a technology described in a single paper, but as a platform. It combines miniature pneumatic hardware, sensors, and software in a modular system that enables not only researchers, but also students, artists, and makers, to develop soft robotics projects more easily.

    Dr. Shtarbanov also founded SoftRobotics.IO, an online community where people can share projects, propose new modules and software, find collaborators, and extend one another’s work. For him, building this community and enabling other people to create with the technology are themselves part of the research.

    Turning an idea into a technically sophisticated paper is difficult. But unpacking the highly developed idea contained in that paper and turning it back into a form that other people can understand, obtain, deploy, and extend is far more demanding and rewarding.

    According to Dr. Shtarbanov, the MIT Media Lab takes a very different approach to research from many other departments.

    “Others typically take a top-down approach to research, where they have an objective to publish first and then develop their project for the sake of publication. At the Media Lab, we often start by just building something first, without much consideration of what field it would fall into - science, engineering, medicine, art, etc. And only when we have something working, we then start asking the question how to disseminate it to the world, what field it would fit into, where it would make sense to publish it, and what other forms of dissemination would also be appropriate - exhibition, website, app, a spin-off, a non-profit entity, TED talk, press-interview, design-competitions, op-ed, etc.

    Of course, the MIT Media Lab is unconventional even by American university standards. Simply transferring its research practices to SNU would not automatically produce the same results.

    What he seeks to bring from the MIT Media Lab to SNU Robotics

    Those expecting advanced new equipment or a large research initiative may be surprised by his answer: “Reogranize the space so it itself fosters more interaction and communication between people; make demos and informal gatherings part of everyday life; host social activities within the lab spaces themselves to enable researchers from different labs to informally meet, talk, and visit each other’s labs; build ecosystems around prominent projects; and use English for all official written and spoken communication within the Institute. These are all parts of the DNA of the MIT Media Lab, and we can replicate them here at SNU RI as well.”

    He suggests starting with something as simple as creating a social area in the most prominent part of the research space, so that people naturally encounter one another while going about their work. He sees this not simply as a social event, but as an initiative with important strategic value: one that builds community and cohesion and can spark new creative ideas. Another Media Lab tradition he hopes to recreate is a scavenger hunt game for incoming researchers. Demos, he argues, should also become part of the mundane, daily experience. They should feel natural and spontaneous rather than being treated as formal presentations or something reserved for special events. At the Media Lab, there is a “demo-and-deploy culture.”

    Declaring a commitment to interdisciplinary research or formally placing researchers from different fields in the same funded project does not necessarily make meaningful collaboration happen. New ideas often emerge only after people repeatedly encounter one another, see what others are working on, and exchange informal questions.

    For Dr. Shtarbanov, sofas, tea hours, and everyday demos are not simply amenities or social activities. They are part of the infrastructure required to build a research ecosystem.

    Where the SNU Robotics Institute’s vision met his own—along with some challenges

    When Dr. Shtarbanov met Director Kyujin Cho and learned about the vision for the SNU Robotics Institute, he became convinced that his own ideas aligned with the Institute’s ambitions and decided to come to SNU.

    Although he has only recently arrived in Korea, he has already experienced some challenges. In a system where researchers are primarily “scored” for research results they produce themselves, thinking about how to expand someone else’s work and create broader impact can sometimes appear to be a luxury rather than a legitimate part of a researcher’s job. And despite his emphasis on communication and collaboration, few meetings have been conducted in English.

    The culture he hopes to bring from the MIT Media Lab is unconventional even within American universities. The institutional gap is inevitably even greater in a Korean university system built strongly around individual research performance, professors, and separate laboratories.

    Moreover, as a postdoctoral fellow, Dr. Shtarbanov has a limited authority to change the Institute’s evaluation system, budget, or use of space on his own. Whether his vision can become reality will therefore will also largely depend on how willing the SNU Robotics Institute is to accept unfamiliar approaches and uncomfortable questions—and how much room it is prepared to give him to experiment.

    The dream he hopes to make real at the SNU Robotics Institute

    On August 18, Dr. Shtarbanov appeared as the eleventh dreamer in the Dreamers’ Talk at the SNU Robotics Institute’s opening ceremony, held under the theme “Dream to Reality.”

    His dream has always been to make prototyping and innovation in emerging fields faster and more accessible in order to enable creativity to flourish. This is why his PhD focused not only on individual technologies, but also on platforms and creative ecosystems.

    He sees enormous potential for the SNU Robotics Institute to become a global leader, comparable to the MIT Media Lab in terms of reputation and impact. He also sees a large part of his role as helping the Institute reach its full impact potential.

    His dream is large, while his formal authority is limited. But an ecosystem is not something that one person can design and complete alone. It emerges when one person throws an idea into the world, someone from another field catches it, and then sends it in an unexpected new direction.

    Enabling SNU’s outstanding robotics research to move beyond publications and continue into other fields of research, technology, industry, and art—this is the impact Dr. Shtarbanov hopes to create.

    Perhaps the largest platform he hopes to build at SNU is not another robot, but the research institute itself: a place where research encounters other people and continues to live, grow, and move.

    Five-Part Plan of Action by Dr. Shtarbanov

    If the SNU Robotics Institute is to realize its ambition of becoming a globally influential research institute, I believe there are five things that can be done immediately. None requires the Institute to abandon its existing strengths. Rather, they are relatively simple changes that can make those strengths more visible, connected, and impactful.

    1. Make English the official language of communication

    All official spoken and written communication within the Institute should be conducted in English. This includes meetings, shared documents, calendars, emails, announcements, articles, and especially group chats.

    For an institute that wants to attract and retain international researchers, this is not simply a matter of convenience. It is basic infrastructure. When important information is communicated only in Korean, international researchers are excluded from conversations, decisions, and informal exchanges that their Korean colleagues take for granted. It directly reduces productivity and makes it much harder for foreign researchers to become fully integrated into the research community.

    This is arguably the simplest and most important change the Institute can make toward becoming genuinely international. It does not require a new building, new equipment, or a new funding program. It simply requires establishing a clear institutional norm and consistently following it.

    2. Design the physical environment to encourage interaction

    The physical layout of the Institute should actively encourage people to encounter one another.

    A prominent social area—with sofas, a coffee table, board games, and perhaps a foosball table—should be added to the research space, and be in the most prominent area of the space, rather than hidden in a separate lounge. People should be able to see the space from their desks and immediately recognize when others are there. This creates opportunities for spontaneous conversations that otherwise would never happen.

    The space should also be designed as a point of attraction for researchers from other laboratories. A visible activity such as foosball can serve a strategic purpose: someone passing through the Institute might stop to play, meet researchers, see a demonstration, and discover work that they would otherwise never encounter.

    The demos and social area should therefore become focal points of the Institute. Both provide natural destinations for people taking breaks, and both create opportunities for researchers to encounter new projects and new people outside their immediate circles.

    The goal is not to make the Institute more comfortable for its own sake. It is to use the physical environment as social infrastructure for research.

    3. Create recurring mechanisms for interdisciplinary interaction

    Simply putting researchers from different fields in the same building does not guarantee interdisciplinary collaboration. People need mechanisms that repeatedly bring them into contact with one another.

    I propose starting with several simple initiatives:

    1. Scavenger Hunt Project Finding Game— A tradition we have at the Media Lab is for incoming students to do a scavenger hunt game on their first day, where they have to walk around all the labs and find as many projects as they can from a list of 50 projects during an afternoon, talk to the researchers that made them, and get a sticker from the corresponding researcher. Whoever collects the most stickers wins and the tops 3 winners get prizes. This game has an important strategic function that right from day one, incoming students become familiar with dozens of researchers at the lab, get to talk to them, and become familiar with their work. It build social cohesion. This also provides a structured way for newcomers to discover the expertise already around them.
    2. Normalize Demoing — Make showing unfinished work to colleagues a routine part of everyday life rather than something reserved for formal presentations or special demo days. The Media Lab has a demo-and-deploy culture that allows people to encounter ideas early, provide feedback, and discover unexpected connections.
    3. Weekly or Biweekly Tea + Snacks — Hold a casual tea-and-snacks hour directly inside the Institute's research space, and invite researchers from other laboratories as well. Different groups can take turns hosting it. The objective is not simply socialization, but to create a recurring opportunity for researchers who would otherwise never meet to encounter one another and do so in a space where they are surrounded by demos which can spark new ideas.
    4. Cross-Lab Project Exchanges — Regularly identify projects, technologies, or research questions that could benefit from expertise elsewhere in the Institute and actively connect the people involved. The Institute should make it easy for a researcher to say, “I saw this project and I think it could be useful for my work.”
    5. Interdisciplinary Free Lunches: People can sign-up to have lunch with someone from another lab in order to foster interdisciplinary interactions. And if they complete the lunch, they get reimbursed for it, up to some limit per year. This fosters community across field boundaries and reimbursement incentivizes people to do it.

    These initiatives are part of the secret-sauce of the Media Lab, and they are quite simple to implement in the SNU RI as well. Interdisciplinary research often begins not with a formal collaboration agreement or proposal, but with a conversation between two people who happened to discover that they were interested in the same problem.

    4. Adopt an ecosystem-centric rather than publication-centric approach to research

    The Institute should measure the success of its research not only by what gets published, but by what happens after publication.

    A publication should be treated as the beginning of dissemination and deployment, not the end of a project. Strong projects should be communicated through project websites, exhibitions, talks, educational materials, open-source repositories, a multidude of applications, spin-offs, replication instructions, social media, press, and collaborations with organizations and people outside academia.

    This also means deliberately reaching beyond the field of robotics. A robotics project may have enormous value to an HCI researcher, designer, artist, educator, materials scientist, or entrepreneur who would never encounter the work through a robotics conference or journal.

    And Korea offers an especially unusual opportunity. Seoul is home to a huge concentration of globally influential cultural figures and media organizations. The Institute should explore collaborations with Korean celebrities, creators, artists, and other public figures who could introduce technologies developed at SNU to audiences far beyond the traditional academic community.

    But dissemination is only the first step.

    Research projects should not be abandoned once their papers are published. This is often when the real work of creating impact begins.

    Conversations with students have revealed that many past projects and demos become extremely difficult to replicate after the original researcher graduates. The tacit knowledge required to rebuild a system leaves with that person. As a result, when a new researcher wants to build upon an earlier project, they just start from scratch because tacit knowledge is not well preserved.

    The Institute should identify its most valuable projects and deliberately build ecosystems around them. This entails documenting them thoroughly, making hardware and software accessible, creating replication instructions, maintaining online infrastructure, developing modular extensions, supporting users, and encouraging communities of researchers, students, artists, and makers to contribute new applications.

    The objective is to create a chain in which one project generates another project, which generates another, and so on. This is the “posterity impact” that allows the influence of a research project to continue growing long after its original creators have moved on.

    5. Bring in top talent from diverse fields and with diverse international perspectives

    Finally, the Institute should broaden the kinds of people it attracts.

    Robotics naturally requires excellent engineers, but the most interesting future applications of robotics will increasingly emerge at the boundaries between engineering and other fields: HCI, design, art, materials science, medicine, education, architecture, fashion, and many others.

    The Institute should therefore actively recruit outstanding people who do not fit neatly into the traditional robotics profile, including researchers and practitioners from different disciplines, countries, and research cultures. And this is likely the easiest part of this plan.

    If the first four pieces are successfully put into place, the talent pool would naturally become larger and more diverse. An institute that communicates in English, provides an unusually collaborative environment, makes its research accessible to the world, builds ecosystems around its projects, and develops a reputation for actually turning research into impact will become a much more attractive destination for exceptional people from around the world.

    The five parts are therefore not independent initiatives. They reinforce one another:

    Communication enables participation. The physical environment enables encounters. Interactions enable collaboration. Ecosystems enable impact. And impact attracts talent.

    Together, they can help transform the SNU Robotics Institute from a collection of excellent laboratories into a genuinely connected research ecosystem—one in which ideas do not simply get published, but continue to move, evolve, and generate new ideas long after the original research is finished.

    Pushing Exoskeletons Out of the Lab and into the Wild: “Smart Apparel” to Support Resilient Mobility Across the Lifespan

    Gregory S. Sawicki, Ph.D. (Woodruff Endowed Professor, Georgia Institute of Technology)

    This talk introduces physiologically inspired ankle and hip exoskeletons designed to improve walking economy, balance, and mobility for both healthy individuals and people with mobility impairments. It also highlights recent research combining wearable sensing and AI to advance wearable robotics from laboratory settings to real-world smart-apparel applications.

    Dr. Sawicki is a Woodruff Endowed Professor with appointments in the Schools of Mechanical Engineering and Biological Sciences at Georgia Tech. He serves as Interim Executive Director of the Institute for Robotics and Intelligent Machines (IRIM) and directs the Human Physiology of Wearable Robotics (PoWeR) Laboratory. His research combines engineering, physiology, and neuroscience to develop lower-limb wearable robots that improve human locomotion.

    Data-Driven Exoskeleton Control Enables Generalized Assistance for Mobility-Impaired Populations

    Aaron Young, Ph.D. (Associate Professor, Woodruff School of Mechanical Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology)

    This talk presents data-driven control approaches for wearable exoskeletons that support people with mobility impairments. It will review two clinical trials using hip and ankle exoskeletons for post-stroke gait impairment, comparing their effects on metabolic cost, biomechanics, clinical outcomes, and user experience.

    Dr. Young is an Associate Professor and Woodruff Faculty Fellow at Georgia Tech, where he directs the Exoskeleton and Prosthetic Intelligent Controls (EPIC) Lab. His research integrates machine learning, robotics, biomechanics, and control systems to develop wearable robotic devices that improve mobility for individuals with walking disabilities.

    [SNU Robotics Seminar] From Neuroscience to Navigation by Michael Milford (QUT)

    ← 소식 전체 보기

    Title: From Neuroscience to Navigation for Autonomous Vehicles and Learnings Along the Way

    Speaker: Michael Milford (Professor at QUT, Australia)

    Time and Date: October 12, 2026 (Monday), 11:00 AM

    Location: Room 101, Building 303

    Abstract

    For roboticists, nature is an amazing inspiration: animals, insects and humans are capable of amazing feats that are currently far beyond the capabilities of robots. Over two decades, our research group has drawn inspiration from nature’s best navigation systems to create high-performance navigation systems for robots like autonomous vehicles. Our inspiration is twofold: we work with neuroscientists who study the neural mechanisms underpinning navigation in the brain, but also look at navigation behaviours, whether it be an ant moving over a sand dune or a rat navigating a maze. But beyond natural inspiration, we also incorporate conventional and learning-based approaches, for three key reasons: 1) “Dogs don’t drive” – many of the tasks we’d like robots to do don’t have direct analogues in nature 2) “Sharks don’t have lasers on their heads” – roboticists can leverage sensing and compute capabilities that now surpass natural systems in some respects and 3) “Much is still not known” – there are still many mysteries of nature and the brain that neuroscientists and biologists are trying to solve – in the meantime, roboticists need to fill in the gaps. It has been an exciting but bumpy career journey, especially early on, moving from fundamental research inspiration to industry collaboration, and working on on-road and off-road autonomous vehicle technology for exotic locations like underground mine sites. We’ve learnt much along the way about how robotics research is performed and evaluated, and the limitations of current benchmarks and metrics for predicting the eventual utility of research that starts in the lab. In this talk, I’ll take the audience on a journey of inspiration, breakthroughs, frustration, and unsolved questions in the quest to develop better robot navigation systems and in doing so, better understand how we ourselves navigate the world.

    Bio

    Michael conducts interdisciplinary fundamental and applied research at the boundary between robotics, neuroscience, computer vision and machine learning, specializing in positioning and localization. From 2022–2027 he is leading a large research team combining bio-inspired and computer science-based approaches to provide a ubiquitous alternative to GPS that does not rely on satellites. His team has worked on patented, award-winning commercial autonomous vehicle navigation technology with companies like Ford and Caterpillar, and been funded by and/or collaborated with organizations like Amazon, Intel and Google Deepmind. He is also one of Australia’s most in demand experts in technologies including self-driving cars, robotics and artificial intelligence, and is a passionate science communicator and mentor. Michael currently holds the position of Director of the QUT Centre for Robotics, Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow, Fellow of the Australian Academy of Technology and Engineering, and is one of only three Australians ever to become a Microsoft Research Faculty Fellow. He recently won the 2025 Eureka Prize for Outstanding Mentor of Researchers.

    [Robotics Seminar] Prof. Zeynep Temel (CMU RI)

    ← 소식 전체 보기

    Adaptive robotics systems using embodied intelligence

    Speaker : Prof. Zeynep Temel

    (Robotics Institute, Carnegie Mellon University)

    Time and Date : November 5, 2026 (Thursday), 13:30

    Location : Room 601, Building 312

    Abstract

    Current robots are primarily rigid machines that exist in highly constrained or open environments such as factory floors, warehouses, or fields. There is an increasing demand for more adaptable, mobile, and flexible robots that can manipulate or move through complex environments. This problem is currently being addressed in two complementary ways: (i) learning and control algorithms to enable the robot to better sense and adapt to the surrounding environment and (ii) embedded intelligence in mechanical structures. My vision is to create robots that can mechanically conform to the environment or objects that they interact with to alleviate the need for high-speed, high-accuracy, and high-precision controllers. In this talk, I will give an overview of our key challenges and contributions to developing mechanically conformable robots, including compliant dexterous manipulation and heterogenous collaborative robots.

    Bio

    Zeynep Temel is an Associate Professor with the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. Her research focuses on developing robots that can mechanically conform to the environment or objects that they interact with. Prior to joining RI, she was a postdoctoral Fellow at the Microrobotics Lab in Harvard University and she received her Ph.D. from Sabanci University, Turkey. In 2020, she was selected as one of 25 members of the Young Scientists Community of World Economic Forum.

    현재의 로봇은 대부분 단단한 구조로 제작되며, 공장·물류창고·야외처럼 조건이 제한되거나 개방된 환경에서 활용되고 있습니다. 그러나 복잡한 환경을 이동하고 물체를 조작하려면 더욱 유연하고 기동성 있으며 상황에 적응할 수 있는 로봇이 필요합니다. 이러한 과제는 크게 두 가지 방향에서 다뤄지고 있습니다. 첫째는 로봇이 주변 환경을 더 정확하게 감지하고 적응하도록 하는 학습·제어 알고리즘이며, 둘째는 기계 구조 자체에 지능을 내재시키는 방법입니다. Temel 교수는 로봇이 접촉하는 환경이나 물체에 기계적으로 형태를 맞춤으로써 고속·고정확도·고정밀 제어에 대한 의존도를 줄이는 로봇을 연구하고 있습니다. 이번 세미나에서는 환경에 유연하게 적응하는 로봇을 개발하는 과정의 주요 과제와 연구 성과를 소개합니다. 순응형 정교 조작과 서로 다른 형태·기능을 가진 로봇들의 협업 연구도 함께 다룰 예정입니다.

    Zeynep Temel 교수는 카네기멜런대학교 로보틱스연구소 부교수로, 환경이나 물체에 기계적으로 유연하게 적응하는 로봇을 연구하고 있습니다. 카네기멜런대학교에 부임하기 전 하버드대학교 마이크로로보틱스연구실에서 박사후연구원으로 근무했으며, 튀르키예 사반즈대학교에서 박사학위를 받았습니다. 2020년에는 세계경제포럼이 선정한 젊은 과학자 커뮤니티의 25인 중 한 명으로 선정되었습니다.

      국가연구소

      국가연구소(NRL 2.0)

      인간중심 피지컬 AI 로보틱스 연구소

      국가연구소 사업

      국가연구소(NRL 2.0)는 교육부와 과학기술정보통신부가 공동으로 추진하는 대학 부설연구소 육성 사업입니다. 서울대학교 로보틱스연구소는 2026년 이 사업에 선정되어, 최대 10년간의 장기 지원을 바탕으로 「인간중심 피지컬 AI 로보틱스 연구소」 과제를 수행합니다. 국가연구소는 로보틱스연구소가 수행하는 연구사업으로, 공학·의학·보건학·뇌인지과학·사회과학 등 여러 분야의 연구진이 함께 참여합니다.

      4 · 3Technical Core · Project Group78교수진 (참여 41 · 연계 37)
      2026–2035최대 10년 장기 지원 · 로봇 분야 유일

      연구 목표

      서울대학교 로보틱스연구소는 이 사업을 통해 로봇의 몸과 지능을 함께 설계하는 인간중심 피지컬 AI 원천기술을 연구합니다. 로봇의 모든 판단과 제어를 중앙의 AI에 집중하는 방식은 복잡한 실제 환경에서 연산량, 에너지 소비, 반응 속도에 한계가 있습니다. 이 과제는 소재와 구조, 접촉과 변형이 계산과 적응의 일부를 담당하는 체화된 물리지능과, 로봇의 각 부위가 정보를 처리하고 학습하며 상위 지능과 협력하는 분산지능을 결합합니다. 이를 통해 환경과 사용자에 적응하는 로봇의 설계·학습·제어 원리를 개발하는 것이 목표입니다.

      인간중심이라는 목표는 로봇의 기능뿐 아니라 사람이 로봇을 사용하는 조건을 연구한다는 뜻입니다. 안전성, 임상적 신뢰성, 사용자 자율성, 사회적 수용성을 설계 단계부터 반영하고 평가합니다. 로봇·인간·환경의 상호작용을 재현하는 디지털 트윈과 실제 실험을 연계해 기술의 성능과 적용 가능성을 검증합니다.

      연구 체계

      Technical Core(TC)는 여러 응용에 공통으로 필요한 원천기술을 개발하고, Project Group(PG)은 사용 환경과 연구 요구를 구체화하며 기술을 적용·검증합니다.

      TC 1MORPHI Body소재·구조의 물리적 특성을 활용하는 적응형 로봇 몸체TC 2MOSAIC Intelligence국소 지능과 전역 지능이 협력하는 분산지능TC 3Digital Twin로봇·인간·환경의 설계, 학습, 검증을 위한 디지털 트윈TC 4Human Value안전성, 임상적 신뢰성, 사회적 수용성의 평가PG 1Life Companion생활 공간에서 사용자의 의도와 환경 변화에 적응하는 일상 지원 로봇PG 2Wearable사람의 동작·힘·균형을 보조하거나 확장하는 웨어러블 로봇PG 3Intra-Body인체 내부 환경과 상호작용하는 로봇 및 진단·치료용 인터페이스

      연구성과의 실증과 사업화

      공통 원천기술을 실제 사용 환경에 적용하고, 실증 결과를 다시 기술 개발에 반영하는 연구 체계를 지향합니다. 연구성과가 연구실에 머무르지 않도록 제작·데이터·컴퓨팅 등 공동 연구 기반을 마련하고, 산학협력과 기술사업화·창업을 연계하는 Lab-to-Market 체계를 추진합니다.

      국가연구소

      TC + PG

      국가연구소의 연구는 두 축이 맞물려 진행됩니다. TC(Technical Core, 핵심기술)는 로봇의 몸과 지능, 디지털 트윈, 인간 가치에 이르는 공통 원천기술을 개발하고, PG(Project Groups, 프로젝트 그룹)는 일상생활 지원, 웨어러블, 체내 로봇처럼 사람을 중심에 둔 응용 문제를 맡습니다. PG가 풀어야 할 문제를 제시하면 TC가 그 해법이 되는 기술을 제공합니다.

      TC 1 MORPHI BodyTC 2 MOSAIC IntelligenceTC 3 Digital TwinTC 4 Human ValuePG 1 Life CompanionPG 2 WearablePG 3 Intra-Body

      Research architecture

      3 Project Group × 4 Technical Core

      모든 Project Group은 네 Technical Core와 협력합니다. 표는 개별 과제의 고정된 배분이 아니라 연구 체계 전체의 연결 구조를 보여줍니다.

      Project Group ↓ · Technical Core →TC 1MORPHI BodyTC 2MOSAIC IntelligenceTC 3Digital TwinTC 4Human Value
      PG 1Life Companion몸의 적응형태·강성상황 이해의도·행동생활 환경가상·실제 검증안전·수용일상 신뢰
      PG 2Wearable신체 인터페이스착용·구동개인 적응움직임·보조사람·로봇 모델설계·평가인간 중심성안전·편의
      PG 3Intra-Body유연한 구조협소 환경 적응정밀 제어상태·행동 조정생체 환경 모델임상 검증임상 신뢰위험·윤리

      PG는 사람 중심의 응용 문제를 제시하고, TC는 하드웨어부터 지능·검증·가치 기준까지 공동 원천기술을 제공합니다.

      Technical Core (TC)

      TC 01 · MORPHI Body

      적응형 로봇 소재·구조 및 물리 지능 연구

      연구 필요성

      사람과 접촉하며 움직이는 로봇은 예측하기 어려운 환경 변화에 안전하게 대응해야 합니다. 모든 반응을 센서와 복잡한 제어 알고리즘으로 처리하면 연산량과 에너지 소비가 커집니다. 고정된 몸체의 한계를 넘어, 소재와 구조 자체가 힘을 분산하고 환경에 순응하도록 만드는 기술이 필요한 이유입니다.

      연구 방향

      MORPHI Body는 환경에 맞게 형태와 강성이 달라지는 가변 구조에 물리 지능을 결합합니다. 메커니즘 자체가 균형을 찾고 힘을 배분하도록 설계해 몸이 연산과 제어의 일부를 분담하게 하고, 로봇이 자신의 신체 상태를 감지해 변화에 대응하도록 연구합니다. 이를 통해 사람과 안전하게 상호작용하면서도 저비용·저전력으로 활용할 수 있는 로봇 하드웨어를 개발하고자 합니다.

      주요 연구 내용

      • 구동·구조 가변 모듈: 형태와 강성을 능동적으로 조절하는 관절 및 생체모사 인공근육 개발
      • 자가 인식 센싱·피부 모듈: 유연한 분산 촉각 센서와 신체 상태 모니터링 기술 개발
      • 모듈화와 신뢰성 검증: 저비용·저전력 하드웨어의 공통 규격 및 내구성·신뢰성 평가 체계 연구

      TC 02 · MOSAIC Intelligence

      분산 지능 모듈의 협력 및 지속 학습 연구

      연구 필요성

      로봇의 몸체나 작업 환경이 달라질 때마다 지능 전체를 다시 학습시키는 방식은 시간과 연산 자원을 많이 요구합니다. 실제 환경에서는 사람과의 접촉이나 작업 조건의 변화에도 즉각 대응해야 하므로, 필요한 기능을 독립적으로 학습하고 재구성하면서 전체 행동을 조율할 수 있는 지능 구조가 필요합니다.

      연구 방향

      MOSAIC Intelligence는 뇌의 기능별 전문성과 조율 구조를 참고해, 부위와 기능별 국소 지능을 상위의 전역 지능이 조율하는 아키텍처를 연구합니다. 국소 지능은 물리적 상호작용과 운동을 학습하고, 전역 지능은 상황과 목표를 판단해 모듈의 협력을 이끕니다. 필요한 모듈을 재조합하고 국소·전역 지능이 함께 지속적으로 학습하도록 하여, 다양한 몸체와 작업에 효율적으로 적응하는 로봇 지능을 개발하고자 합니다.

      주요 연구 내용

      • 자율형 국소 지능: 로봇·인간·환경의 물리적 특성을 인식하고 독립적으로 운동을 학습하는 모듈 개발
      • 맥락적 전역 지능: 상황을 이해하고 예측하며 여러 인식·운동 모듈을 조율하는 지능 개발
      • 지속 학습과 공진화: 국소·전역 지능이 상호 보완적으로 학습하고 새로운 환경과 임무에 적응하는 구조 연구

      TC 03 · Digital Twin

      로봇·인간·환경 디지털 트윈

      연구 필요성

      사람과 로봇이 접촉하고 주변 환경이 변하는 상황을 다루려면 여러 물리현상을 함께 예측해야 합니다. 기존의 디지털 트윈은 현상별로 분리되어 있거나, 예측 정확도를 높일수록 계산 속도가 느려지는 한계가 있습니다. 로봇의 설계·학습·검증을 가속하려면 복잡한 상호작용을 정확하고 빠르게 모사하면서 다양한 데이터를 일관되게 관리할 수 있어야 합니다.

      연구 방향

      로봇·인간·환경 디지털 트윈은 다중물리 시뮬레이션, 데이터 패브릭, 소프트웨어·하드웨어 통합 최적화를 연결합니다. 가상실험에서 물리적으로 타당한 데이터를 생성·증강하고, 실제 환경에서 얻은 데이터와 연계해 로봇을 반복적으로 설계하고 검증하는 기반을 연구합니다. 생활 지원, 웨어러블, 체내 로봇의 서로 다른 조건에 활용할 수 있는 통합 프레임워크를 개발하고자 합니다.

      주요 연구 내용

      • 디지털 트윈: 복잡한 물리적 상호작용의 고정밀·고속 모사 및 학습·검증용 데이터 생성
      • 데이터 패브릭: 물리적 정합성과 맥락을 유지하며 다양한 형식의 대규모 데이터를 생성·증강·저장·관리
      • 인프라 최적화: 시뮬레이션과 데이터 처리를 효율적으로 구동하는 소프트웨어·하드웨어 통합 설계

      TC 04 · Human Value

      로봇의 안전성·임상적 신뢰성 및 사회적 수용성

      연구 필요성

      로봇의 성능이 높아지는 것만으로 사람에게 유익하고 신뢰할 수 있는 기술이 되는 것은 아닙니다. 사람의 신체와 일상에 직접 개입하는 로봇은 안전뿐 아니라 기능과 자율성 등 인간의 가치를 함께 고려해야 합니다. 개발이 끝난 뒤 윤리나 사용성을 평가하는 데 그치지 않고, 초기 설계부터 제어와 실증까지 그 가치를 반영하고 검증하는 체계가 필요합니다.

      연구 방향

      Human Value는 인간 중심 가치를 설계 판단과 제어 원칙으로 구체화하고, 개발 전 과정에서 검증할 수 있는 가치 운영체계(Value OS)를 연구합니다. 임상·사회적 맥락을 반영한 시나리오에서 로봇의 행동과 가치 훼손 위험을 점검하며, 평가 결과를 다음 설계에 반영합니다. 이를 통해 로봇의 임상적 신뢰성과 사회적 수용성을 일관된 기준으로 비교·판단할 수 있는 기반을 마련하고자 합니다.

      주요 연구 내용

      • 가치 기반 설계: 안전·기능·자율성 등의 지표를 정의하고 설계 및 검증 기준으로 활용
      • 실증과 스트레스 테스트: 다양한 상호작용 조건에서 가치 훼손 임계점을 탐지하고 판단 근거를 설명
      • 공통 기준과 설계 환류: Human Value API와 신뢰성 판단 기준을 연구하고 평가 결과를 제어·설계 개선에 반영

      PG 02 · Wearable

      신체 움직임 보조·증강 웨어러블 로봇 연구

      사람의 신체와 직접 맞닿는 로봇으로 움직임과 힘, 균형을 보조하고 개인의 신체 특성에 맞는 자연스러운 착용 경험을 구현합니다.

      • 신체 움직임과 사용자의 의도를 반영하는 보조 기술
      • 착용감·구동 성능을 함께 고려하는 개인 맞춤형 설계
      • 사람과 로봇의 상호작용 데이터를 활용한 설계·평가

      PG 03 · Intra-Body

      인체 내부 작동 로봇 연구

      좁고 민감한 체내 환경에서 주변 조직과 조화를 이루며 작동하는 로봇과 인터페이스를 연구하고, 의료 현장과 연결되는 검증 기반을 구축합니다.

      • 협소하고 복잡한 환경에 대응하는 유연·적응형 구조
      • 생체 환경과 로봇의 상호작용을 고려한 정밀 동작
      • 안전성과 임상적 신뢰를 갖춘 실증·평가 방법

      학부생을 위한 로봇 제작 수업

      창의공학설계

      수업 소개

      창의공학설계(창공)는 서울대학교 기계공학부 신입생들이 팀을 이루어 직접 로봇을 설계하고 제작하는 프로젝트 기반 수업으로, 1993년 故 주종남 교수가 처음 도입한 이후 30년 넘게 이어지며 서울대학교 공과대학의 대표적인 공학교육으로 자리 잡았습니다. 학생들은 주어진 임무를 수행하는 로봇을 구상하고, 제한된 조건 안에서 직접 만들고 시험하며 문제를 해결하는 과정에서 창의성과 팀워크, 공학적 문제 해결 능력을 기릅니다. 수업 내용은 기술 발전을 반영해 꾸준히 바뀌어 왔으며, 2024년부터는 AI 로봇 아키텍처 교육의 기반으로 원격 장치를 도입했습니다.

      1993첫 수업 · 故 주종남 교수
      30회2022년 제30회 로보콘
      12주차직접 만든 로봇으로 로보콘 본 경기

      교육과정

      창의공학설계

      이 과목은 다양하게 주어진 목표물을 직접 설계하고 제작하는 실습을 통해 설계와 제작에 대한 기본 감각과 창의성을 키우는 데 목적이 있다. 아직 공학의 개념이 확립되지 않은 1학년 학생을 대상으로, 정해진 재료로 제품을 직접 만들고 그것으로 경기를 해 봄으로써 흥미를 가지고 공학의 의미를 체험하도록 한다. 제품은 여러 공학 분야의 특성을 종합적으로 표현할 수 있는 기구, 구조물 등 다양한 대상이 된다. 코딩과 하드웨어 경험이 부족한 학생도 입문 단계부터 단계적으로 학습할 수 있도록 구성하였다.

      1. 매주강의 2시간 · 실습 2시간
      2. 1–6주설계 기본원칙 · 기구학 · 가공방법 강의, 로봇 프로그래밍 실습과 제작
      3. 7주설계·제작할 로봇의 용도와 규칙 발표
      4. 12주제공된 재료와 도구로 규칙 안에서 자유롭게 설계·제작한 로봇으로 로보콘 본 경기

      기계시스템 설계와 로봇 프로그래밍의 기초

      창의공학설계를 듣기 전에 반드시 먼저 들어야 하는 준비 과목입니다.

      본 과목에서는 기계시스템 설계의 기본 개념과 방법에 대해 익히고 기계시스템의 구동을 위해 필수적인 로봇 프로그래밍의 기초를 배운다. 구체적으로, 설계 도면에 대한 이해와 설계안을 구체화하는 도면 작성법, 컴퓨터 이용 설계(Computer-Aided-Design, CAD) 프로그램을 이용한 설계 방법을 배운다. 이후 기계시스템을 지능적으로 구동하기 위한 프로그래밍을 학습한다. Matlab, python, C/C++ 등 다양한 프로그래밍 언어와 이를 통한 로봇 하드웨어 구동을 위한 미들웨어를 학습한다. 학기 말에 최종적으로 소프트웨어, 미들웨어, 하드웨어를 통합한 시스템을 설계한다. 본 과목에서 학습한 설계 및 프로그래밍은 향후 다양한 기계공학 전공과목의 효과적인 학습에 도움이 된다.

      1. 매주강의 2시간 · 실습 2시간 (3학점)
      2. 설계설계 도면의 이해와 작성, CAD를 이용한 설계
      3. 프로그래밍Matlab · Python · C/C++, 로봇 하드웨어 구동을 위한 미들웨어
      4. 학기 말소프트웨어 · 미들웨어 · 하드웨어를 통합한 시스템 설계 프로젝트

      SNU Robocon

      로보콘

      수업의 마지막에는 수강생 전원이 직접 만든 로봇으로 팀별 대항전을 벌이는 로보콘이 열립니다. 로보콘에서 우승한 팀은 국가대표로 국제 로보콘 대회에 출전합니다.
